sceneHappening: Paul defends his authority with the gentleness of Christ, against those who say he is weak
summary: Here the tone changes. "Now I Paul, myself, entreat you by the humility and gentleness of Christ, I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you." He begs them that when he is present he will not need to be bold with the confidence with which he plans to be bold against some who suspect they walk according to the flesh. "For though we walk in the flesh, we don't wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ." He is ready to punish all disobedience when their obedience is complete. "You look at things according to the outward appearance. If anyone is confident in himself that he is Christ's, let him remind himself that, just as he is Christ's, so also are we." Even if Paul boasts somewhat more of the authority the Lord gave for building up and not for tearing down, he will not be ashamed. He does not want to seem to terrify them by letters, for some say, "His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised." Such people should know that what Paul is in word by letters when absent, he will be also in deed when present. He does not dare to classify or compare himself with some who commend themselves; they measure themselves by themselves. But Paul will not boast beyond limits, but within the field God has assigned, which reaches even to them; he did not overextend, for he was first to come all the way to Corinth with the gospel. He hopes that as their faith grows, his area will be greatly enlarged, so that he can preach the gospel in regions beyond them, not boasting in another's field. "But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord." For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
whySettingMatters: Chapters 10 to 13 are written in a very different mood from chapters 1 to 9, and that is the biggest debate about the letter. Some scholars think these chapters are part of a separate letter written after bad news came from Corinth, perhaps the "severe letter" or a later one; others think they belong to the same letter and that Paul turns, after thanking the majority, to the minority still opposing him. The text itself does not decide. What is clear is that outside teachers (the "super-apostles," 11:5) have been criticizing him: his letters are strong but he is unimpressive in person, his speech is poor, and he does not take pay. In a culture that valued polished speaking, that was a serious charge. Paul's answer is that his weapons are spiritual, his authority is for building up, and the right kind of boasting is "in the Lord." The military picture of strongholds and captives comes from the world of Roman warfare. The "field" (kanon) he speaks of is the area of mission assigned to him, probably recalling the agreement with the Jerusalem leaders about who would work among whom (Galatians 2:7-9).

questions: Paul appeals "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ," then talks about weapons and strongholds. How do these fit together?
His critics say he is bold only in letters. How should a leader respond to criticism of that kind?
"Take every thought captive to obey Christ." What are the "strongholds" he has in mind?
"Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord." What makes a boast legitimate in Paul's view?
